label: Cats
note: Exit ticket: Name one noun that takes -es after x, s, ch, or sh (like boxes or dishes).

deep.summary: What you learn: English often marks “more than one” by adding a sound spelled -s or -es. Think of -es as the spelling you reach for when plain -s would feel clumsy after certain endings (like boxes, classes).

etymology.origin: Inflectional ending—does a grammar job (plural or verb agreement), not a “new word family” like Latin prefixes.

deep.tense: Here -s marks plural nouns. The same letters can mark verb agreement (She runs)—sentence context tells you which job.

label: Jumped
note: Exit ticket: Say the word aloud: does -ed come out as /t/, /d/, or an extra syllable /ɪd/?

tree.gloss: verb: did a jump; past time

deep.summary: What you learn: -ed usually signals “already happened” or “finished action,” though English also uses other past forms (went, sang). When it attaches to a regular verb like jump, you get a predictable past form.
deep.tense: Past tense / participle family. Compare irregular pasts for contrast (jumped vs ran).

label: Running
note: Exit ticket: Give a sentence using running as a noun (Running helps…) and one using it as part of a progressive verb.

tree.gloss: verb/noun: the action of run; ongoing action

deep.summary: What you learn: -ing shows up in several grammar roles—ongoing action (is running), a noun-like activity (Running is fun), and adjective-like uses (running water). Same spelling; sentence job differs.
deep.tense: Ask “Is this naming an activity, marking ongoing time, or modifying a noun?”

label: Quickly
note: Exit ticket: Turn happy into an adverb with -ly. What happens to the y?

deep.summary: What you learn: Many English adverbs are built by adding -ly to an adjective—often meaning “in a ___ way.” Watch friendly exceptions (fast can be adjective or adverb without -ly).

etymology.origin: Turns many adjectives into manner adverbs.

label: Teacher
note: Exit ticket: Name another word where -er means “a person who ___s,” and one where -or does the same job (actor, elevator patterns).

deep.summary: What you learn: Here -er builds a noun for a role or doer: “someone who teaches.” Don’t confuse that with comparative -er (faster)—sentence context and the base word’s part of speech usually make it obvious.

etymology.origin: Agentive suffix—person or thing tied to an action.

deep.formation: Parallel pattern with -or after Latin stems (actor, supervisor)—same “doer” idea, different spelling history.

label: Cloudy
note: Exit ticket: What does -y add to the noun cloud here—not plural -ies, but adjective meaning?

tree.gloss: adjective: full of clouds; gray sky

deep.summary: What you learn: This -y builds an adjective from a noun: “cloud-like / having clouds.” Don’t mix this up with plural spellings like clouds—grammar and pronunciation tell them apart.

label: Careful
note: Exit ticket: Pair -ful with -less: what’s the difference between hopeful and hopeless?

deep.summary: What you learn: -ful makes adjectives meaning “full of” or “having.” It clarifies tone—careful is “having care,” not “without care.”

etymology.origin: “Full of” — opposite vibe from -less in many pairs.

label: Unhappy
note: Exit ticket: Why is unhappy usually taught with native Germanic bases, while “not + Latin stem” often uses in- / im- instead?

deep.summary: What you learn: un- often negates or reverses short, everyday bases (unfair, unzip). It’s a different “not” family than Latinate in-, but the reading strategy is similar: strip the prefix and read the base.

etymology.origin: Negation / reversal—listen for bases that feel like everyday English.

label: Reuse
note: Exit ticket: When does re- mean “again,” and when does it feel more like “back” (return, reflect)?

deep.summary: What you learn: re- usually signals repetition or doing something back/again—reading science and history, you’ll see it constantly on verbs (rebuild, review).

etymology.origin: Again / back—exact nuance comes from the base verb.

label: Overlook
note: Exit ticket: Overlook can mean “look down on from above” or “fail to notice”—how does context pick the meaning?

deep.summary: What you learn: Over- can be literal “above” (overhead) or “too much / excess” (overreact). That’s why some over- words have two plausible readings until context pins them down.
deep.tense: Verb—pay attention to idiomatic meanings in reading class.

label: Subway
note: Exit ticket: Where do you find another sub- word that means “under” literally (submarine)?

deep.summary: What you learn: Sub- usually signals “under” or “below rank” (subtract, submarine). In compounds like subway, it tightens what kind of route it is.

embedded.note: Think physically under or hierarchically below.

label: Midnight
note: Exit ticket: Why is midnight “the middle of the night” but clock time can disagree with astronomy?

tree.gloss: noun: middle of the night; 12:00 a.m.

deep.summary: What you learn: Mid- picks the middle of something (midday, midterm). Transparent compounds help spelling—you hear both chunks.

embedded.note: Locates you halfway through the named span.

label: Exit
note: Exit ticket: Find eject or efface and explain how the prefix shortened before the stem.

deep.summary: What you learn: Ex- (and shapes like e-, ef-) often marks “out” or “former” (exit, exclude). Pair it mentally with ad-/in- “toward/in” when you contrast words.

label: Television
note: Exit ticket: Split another word with vid (video, evidence).

deep.summary: What you learn: Vis/vid = see—evidence, video, vision. Television literally “far seeing,” though etymology is more layered than the classroom shortcut.
